sections.h2: What kind of city is Farmington, Minnesota, for a home seller?
sections.html:
Farmington is a small Dakota County city on the southern edge of the Twin Cities area, and most of its housing is owner-occupied. The Census Bureau estimates 25,425 residents as of July 1, 2025, a 7.4 percent gain over the April 2020 base. The city covers about 14.6 square miles of land and borders Lakeville to the west, Empire Township to the east, and Castle Rock and Eureka townships to the south.

Locals divide town roughly along County Highway 50. South of it sits the older downtown, which has seen few big projects in recent decades. North of it, most subdivisions are newer, and a third growth area spreads east into Empire Township. A trail along the Vermillion River links downtown, uptown and the Empire-side neighborhoods, a feature worth mentioning in a listing or an offer conversation.

The city got its charter in 1872, making it the second-oldest community in Dakota County after Hastings. A fire on November 22, 1879 destroyed several houses, stores, a hotel and a grain elevator in the downtown area. Houses here range from century-old downtown homes to subdivision builds from the 2000s, when the population roughly doubled between 2000 and 2010 (from 12,365 to 21,086).

sections.h2: What do Farmington's housing numbers say about my sale?
sections.html:
Farmington homes carry a median value of $366,200 in the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimates, and 86.5 percent of housing units are owner-occupied. A seller here is usually competing with other single-family houses, with few apartments in the mix.

sections.h2: How do I close out the Farmington city water account when I sell?
sections.html:
Call Farmington Utility Billing at 651-280-6883 before closing to book a final meter reading. The city does not shut water off when someone moves out, so the account keeps running until you close it.

  • Utility bills come quarterly, and the city bills water, sewer, storm water and street lights.
  • Trash and recycling are billed separately by Dick's Sanitation, which handles cancellations at 952-469-2239.
  • Any unpaid final utility bill is certified to the property as a special assessment, so a buyer's title company may hold money back at closing if the account is open.

Landlords selling a rental should know that Farmington keeps rental utility accounts in the owner's name, so the owner has to close the account, not the tenant. A late fee of 10 percent applies to rental accounts that fall behind. Ask Utility Billing for the exact balance on your closing date rather than estimating it from the last bill.

sections.h2: Which schools, roads and employers shape buyer interest in Farmington?
sections.html:
Farmington Area Public Schools, Independent School District 192, enrolls about 6,900 students. Its boundaries take in Farmington, the eastern part of Lakeville, and Castle Rock, Empire and Eureka townships, so a buyer's address can matter for which district a family lands in. Most of Lakeville sits in a different district, so check the district for your exact address.

Main routes are Minnesota Highway 3, Minnesota Highway 50, and Dakota County Roads 31 and 50. The Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center is in Farmington, and a Kemps packing plant is another long-standing local employer. The Dakota County Fairgrounds, about 360 acres with entrances on 220th Street and Highway 3, also sit inside the city limits and report the highest county fair attendance in the state.

  • Price point: the $366,200 median value compares with $452,500 in neighboring Lakeville.
  • Commute: the 27.7 minute average drive to work is long for the metro.

sections.h2: What are my options for selling a house fast in Farmington?
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or take a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. Each route trades speed against price and effort.

  • Listing: best when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings, inspections and a buyer's financing.
  • Selling it yourself: saves a commission but leaves marketing, paperwork and negotiation on you.
  • Cash offer: suits inherited houses, homes needing repairs, rentals with tenants, or owners behind on payments, because the buyer takes the property as it stands and closing can be scheduled around your date.

Whichever route you take, Minnesota law requires you to give the buyer a written disclosure of material facts you know about before signing a purchase agreement (Minnesota Statutes 513.55). Farmington's neighborhoods north of County Highway 50 were built mostly in the last two decades, while downtown houses are older, so the condition questions differ by area.

sections.h2: What does Dakota County require to record a Farmington deed?
sections.html:
Dakota County Property Taxation and Records records every deed for the county, and in-person recording happens at the Administration Center in Hastings by appointment. You can also mail documents to 1590 Highway 55, Hastings, MN 55033 with a cover letter, a stamped return envelope and a phone number. Most Dakota County parcels are abstract property, which means a title company searches the record before closing.

State deed tax is the net purchase price multiplied by 0.0033. On a sale at Farmington's $366,200 median value, that works out to about $1,208. Every transfer deed also needs a well disclosure certificate, or the deed must carry the statement that the seller knows of no wells (Minnesota Statutes 103I.235). The county auditor checks for delinquent taxes before a deed is accepted for recording (Minnesota Statutes 272.12).

Dakota County lists its mandated recording fees on its filing fees page, so ask your title company which charges apply to your closing.

sections.h2: How do Dakota County property taxes affect a Farmington closing?
sections.html:
Property tax is paid in two halves, due in mid-May and mid-October. Dakota County's 2026 calendar lists May 15 and October 15, and the second-half date has now passed for this year. State law sets a 2 percent penalty on homestead property and 4 percent on non-homestead property for a missed half, with more added each month through December (Minnesota Statutes 279.01).

Ask your title company to prorate the current year's tax between you and the buyer at closing, and check the county's property information search for any open balance before you list. Homestead applications for the next year are due December 31.

faqs.q: How soon can a Farmington house sale close?
faqs.a: A cash sale can close on whatever date you pick, often within a few weeks, because there is no lender appraisal to wait on. A traditional listing usually takes longer once showings, inspections and the buyer's loan are counted. Book the water meter reading with Farmington Utility Billing before either closing date.

faqs.q: Do I have to make repairs before selling a house in Farmington?
faqs.a: The disclosure statute asks for a written statement of material facts you know before a purchase agreement is signed, and it does not list required repairs. Cash buyers take the house as-is, while retail buyers often negotiate repairs after an inspection.

faqs.q: What happens to unpaid city utility bills when I sell?
faqs.a: They follow the property. Farmington certifies unpaid water, sewer, storm drainage and street light charges to the property as a special assessment, so a buyer's title company will usually want the final bill settled. Request a final read before closing so the bill is accurate.

faqs.q: Who records the deed when I sell a Farmington home?
faqs.a: Dakota County Property Taxation and Records in Hastings records it, usually through your title company. Fees are set by state statute, deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price, and a well disclosure certificate or well statement must accompany the deed.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Farmington rental house with tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Review the lease terms with the buyer and your title company. Because Farmington keeps rental utility accounts in the owner's name, plan to close that account on the sale date and tell the tenants where to send new billing questions.
